name: Polycarp of Smyrna

seo.title: St Polycarp of Smyrna: how he died, his words and feast days
seo.description: Polycarp of Smyrna in plain words: John's hearer and Irenaeus's teacher. How he died in the stadium, his real words, his feast days, and the myths.

band.lede: The old bishop who had known John, and would not curse Christ to save his life.

who: Polycarp was bishop of Smyrna, today Izmir in Turkey, from early in the 100s until his death. He had known John and others who had seen Jesus. Irenaeus heard him as a boy. One letter of his survives. When he was very old, he refused to curse Christ. He died for it in the stadium at Smyrna, about 155.

tidbits.text: The words “the Catholic Church” first appear in a letter to his own church: Ignatius's *Letter to the Smyrnaeans*. In most copies, the account of Polycarp's death uses them four times.

cite.text: Ignatius, Letter to the Smyrnaeans, chapter 8; McGiffert, note on Eusebius, Church History, Book 4, chapter 15

tidbits.text: More than two centuries after he died, his *Letter* was still “read to the present day in the meetings in Asia”, says Jerome.

cite.text: Jerome, Lives of Illustrious Men, chapter 17

tidbits.text: Heinrich Biber's *Sonata Sancti Polycarpi* is written for eight trumpets and timpani. It most likely honoured a Salzburg churchman who bore the saint's name: Polykarp von Khüenburg, the archbishop's nephew. It may have been played on his name day.

cite.text: McNaughtan Publishing, notes to Biber's Sonata Sancti Polycarpi

facts.label: Born
facts.text: About 69 or 70, counting back from the 86 years he spoke of at his trial. No early source says where.

facts.label: Bishop of
facts.text: **Smyrna**, today **Izmir in Turkey**, for decades. Ignatius wrote to him there as its bishop, early in the 100s.

facts.label: Died
facts.text: **23 February**, a Saturday, most likely in **155**. In the stadium at Smyrna. Eusebius put it about ten years later.

facts.label: Buried
facts.text: His body was burned. His church gathered the bones and laid them “in a fitting place”. It does not say where.

facts.label: Also called
facts.text: **Hieromartyr Polycarp**, in the Orthodox churches: a martyr who was a priest or bishop. An **Apostolic Father**, one of the first Christian writers after the apostles.

facts.label: His name
facts.text: From the Greek {el|πολύκαρπος}: fruitful, or “rich in fruit”.

facts.label: Status
facts.text: A saint to Catholics, Orthodox, Copts and Anglicans. Lutherans remember him too.

facts.label: In art
facts.text: The Orthodox painters' guide of Dionysius of Fourna asks for an old man with a rounded beard. Older frescoes, like the one at the top of this page, give him a long white one. In the West, a bishop at the stake, with flames or a pile of wood, or stabbed.

facts.label: Wrote
facts.text: One letter survives, the *Letter to the Philippians*. Irenaeus knew others, now lost.

west.text: His day in the **1916 Roman Martyrology**, and in the Roman calendar until 1969.
**Catholic** memorial, optional when it falls in Lent. Also the **Church of England**, the **Episcopal Church**, and Lutherans in the **Missouri Synod** and the **ELCA**.

east.text: The **OCA**, the **Greek** churches, and the **Russian Church** on the old calendar.
The **Coptic** Church, on 29 Amshir in its own calendar. In most years the Russian Church's 23 February falls on this day too.

feasts.note: Why 23 February? The letter on his death names the day. In Lightfoot's translation it is “the seventh before the kalends of March”. (The *Ante-Nicene Fathers* translation reads “May” here.) Rome kept him on 26 January until 1969. That was the day another Polycarp, of Nicaea, died. The new calendar moved him to the day he died. In the 1916 book, 23 February belonged to yet another Polycarp, a Roman priest. Churches on the old calendar keep each date 13 days later, so 23 February falls on 8 March (7 March in a leap year).

traits.title: brave, but not reckless
traits.text: A Phrygian named Quintus had pushed others to give themselves up with him. When he saw the beasts, he lost his nerve and offered sacrifice. The church of Smyrna drew the lesson: “we do not commend those who give themselves up [to suffering], seeing the Gospel does not teach so to do.” Polycarp was not afraid, but he left the city when his people asked. He moved again when the searchers came near.

traits.title: kind to the men who came for him
traits.text: When the police found him, he came down and talked with them. Then he had food and drink set before them, “as much indeed as they cared for”. Many of them began to wish they had not come.

traits.title: blunt with false teachers
traits.text: Marcion, a teacher who rejected the God of the Old Testament, once met him and asked, “Dost thou know me?” Polycarp answered, “I do know thee, the first-born of Satan.” His own *Letter* says the same of anyone who twists the Lord's words and denies the resurrection: “he is the first-born of Satan”. Irenaeus once told Florinus, who had known Polycarp too, what Polycarp would have done had he heard Florinus's teaching. He would have stopped his ears. He would have cried out, as was his custom, “O good God, unto what times hast Thou spared me that I should endure these things?”

cite.text: Irenaeus, Against Heresies, Book 3, chapter 3; Letter to the Philippians, chapter 7; Irenaeus's letter to Florinus, in Eusebius, Church History, Book 5, chapter 20

traits.title: a man of prayer
traits.text: At the farm where he hid, he did nothing, night and day, but pray “for all men, and for the Churches throughout the world, according to his usual custom”. Years before, Ignatius had told him, “Give thyself to prayer without ceasing.”

cite.text: Martyrdom of Polycarp, chapter 5; Ignatius, Letter to Polycarp, chapter 1

traits.title: gentle with the fallen
traits.text: Valens, once a presbyter at Philippi, had done wrong, most likely out of greed. Polycarp wrote, “I am deeply grieved, therefore, brethren, for him (Valens) and his wife; to whom may the Lord grant true repentance!” He told the church not to treat them as enemies, but to “call them back as suffering and straying members”.

traits.title: true to what he was taught
traits.text: He always taught what he had learned from the apostles, says Irenaeus, “and which the Church has handed down, and which alone are true”. His own *Letter* says the same: “let us return to the word which has been handed down to us from the beginning”.

cite.text: Irenaeus, Against Heresies, Book 3, chapter 3; Letter to the Philippians, chapter 7

traits.title: honoured by his own people
traits.text: At the pyre he took off his own clothes, and tried to take off his own sandals. He was not used to doing it. The faithful always rushed to do it for him, each one “eager who should first touch his skin”. In Lightfoot's words, he had been honoured for his holy life “even before his gray hairs came”.

cite.text: Martyrdom of Polycarp, chapter 13; the last line in Lightfoot's translation (1891)

traits.title: humble
traits.text: He wrote to Philippi only because they had asked him to, he said. And he knew his place: “For neither I, nor any other such one, can come up to the wisdom of the blessed and glorified Paul.”

said.lede: We have a letter written to him by Ignatius, a letter of his own, his church's account of his death, and the memories of a boy who heard him teach.

quotes.q: Having obtained good proof that thy mind is fixed in God as upon an immoveable rock, I loudly glorify [His name] that I have been thought worthy [to behold] thy blameless face.
quotes.who: Ignatius of Antioch, a prisoner on his way to die in Rome

quotes.q: Stand firm, as does an anvil which is beaten. It is the part of a noble athlete to be wounded, and yet to conquer.
…a man who was of much greater weight, and a more stedfast witness of truth, than Valentinus, and Marcion, and the rest of the heretics.
quotes.who: Irenaeus, who heard him as a boy

quotes.q: For in Asia also great lights have fallen asleep, which shall rise again on the day of the Lord's coming, when He shall come with glory from heaven, and shall seek out all the saints. … And Polycarp in Smyrna, who was a bishop and martyr.
quotes.who: Polycrates, bishop of Ephesus, about 190, writing to Rome about the date of Easter

quotes.q: This is the teacher of Asia, the father of the Christians, and the overthrower of our gods, he who has been teaching many not to sacrifice, or to worship the gods.
quotes.who: The crowd in the stadium, shouting for his death

quotes.q: …an apostolic and prophetic teacher, and bishop of the Catholic Church which is in Smyrna. For every word that went out of his mouth either has been or shall yet be accomplished.
quotes.who: His church at Smyrna, after his death

moments.title: Taught by those who saw Jesus
moments.text: Polycarp learned from apostles, says Irenaeus, and “conversed with many who had seen Christ”. He used to tell what John and the others had told him of the Lord, His miracles and His teaching. Irenaeus says he told it all “in harmony with the Scriptures”.

cite.text: Irenaeus, Against Heresies, Book 3, chapter 3; Eusebius, Church History, Book 5, chapter 20

moments.title: John at the bath-house
moments.text: Polycarp told a story about John. At Ephesus, John went to the public baths and saw Cerinthus inside, a teacher he held to be false. He rushed out without bathing. “Let us fly, lest even the bath-house fall down, because Cerinthus, the enemy of the truth, is within.” Irenaeus had the story from people who heard Polycarp tell it.

moments.title: A prisoner passes through
moments.text: Ignatius, bishop of Antioch, was being taken under guard to Rome, to be thrown to the beasts. His guards stopped at Smyrna, where Polycarp was bishop. From there Ignatius wrote four letters. Later, from Troas, he wrote to the church of Smyrna and to Polycarp himself. He gave him a bishop's advice: “Bear with all, even as the Lord does with thee.” He asked him to write to the churches he had no time to reach. And, says Eusebius, he “commended to him, like a true and good shepherd, the flock at Antioch”.

cite.text: Eusebius, Church History, Book 3, chapter 36; Ignatius, Letter to Polycarp, chapters 1 and 8

moments.title: His one surviving letter
moments.text: The church at Philippi asked him for a letter of advice, and for copies of Ignatius's letters. He sent both. “The Epistles of Ignatius written by him to us, and all the rest [of his Epistles] which we have by us, we have sent to you, as you requested.” He asked them for any news of Ignatius and the men with him. The collection he sent is probably how Ignatius's letters survive at all. Some scholars have thought these lines about Ignatius a later addition. Its Victorian translators, Roberts and Donaldson, saw “considerable force” in their case. McGiffert called its rejection “quite arbitrary”.

cite.text: Letter to the Philippians, chapter 13; Ante-Nicene Fathers, volume 1, introductory note; McGiffert, note on Eusebius, Church History, Book 4, chapter 14; Lightfoot, The Apostolic Fathers, Part 2, volume 1 (1889)

moments.title: A boy in the audience
moments.text: Irenaeus heard Polycarp as a boy, and later became bishop of Lyons. Decades on, he wrote that he remembered those days better than recent years: “I am able to describe the very place in which the blessed Polycarp sat as he discoursed, and his goings out and his comings in, and the manner of his life, and his physical appearance.” He had kept Polycarp's words “not on paper, but in my heart”.

cite.text: Letter to Florinus, in Eusebius, Church History, Book 5, chapter 20

moments.title: Agreeing to differ
moments.text: Near the end of his life, Polycarp was in Rome while Anicetus was its bishop. Jerome says he came “on account of certain questions concerning the day of the Passover”. The two also “disagreed a little about certain other things”. Polycarp kept Easter as he had kept it “with John the disciple of our Lord, and the other apostles”. Anicetus followed “the presbyters that had preceded him” in Rome. Neither could persuade the other. They stayed in communion anyway. As a mark of respect, Anicetus let Polycarp celebrate the Eucharist in his own church. Then they “parted from each other in peace”. While in Rome, says Irenaeus, Polycarp turned many followers of Valentinus and Marcion back to the Church.

cite.text: Irenaeus's letter to Victor, in Eusebius, Church History, Book 5, chapter 24; Jerome, Lives of Illustrious Men, chapter 17; Against Heresies, Book 3, chapter 3

moments.title: The crowd calls for him
moments.text: There were games at Smyrna, and Christians were being put to death in the arena. A young man named Germanicus faced the beasts so bravely that he drew one toward himself. The crowd marvelled at the Christians' courage. Then it turned on their old bishop: “Away with the Atheists; let Polycarp be sought out!” Christians were called atheists because they would not honour the gods.

moments.title: Hidden, then betrayed
moments.text: He meant to stay in the city, but his people persuaded him to leave. He stayed at a farm nearby with a few friends. When the searchers came near, he moved to another. They seized two young servants, and one of them confessed under torture. “It was thus impossible that he should continue hid, since those that betrayed him were of his own household.”

moments.title: Two hours of prayer
moments.text: Police and horsemen came on the Friday evening. He was in an upper room, and he could have slipped away. He would not. “The will of God be done,” he said, and went down to them. They marvelled at his age. He asked for an hour to pray, and then stood and prayed for two full hours. He named everyone who had ever come his way, “both small and great, illustrious and obscure, as well as the whole Catholic Church throughout the world”.

moments.title: In Herod's carriage
moments.text: They set him on a donkey and led him into the city, on the day of “the great Sabbath”. Herod, the police captain, and his father Nicetes took him into their carriage and tried to talk him round. “What harm is there in saying, Lord Cæsar, and in sacrificing, with the other ceremonies observed on such occasions, and so make sure of safety?” At first he said nothing. Then: “I shall not do as you advise me.” They threw him out so roughly that he hurt his shin. He walked on quickly, “as if suffering nothing”.

moments.title: Before the proconsul
moments.text: The noise in the stadium was so great that no one could be heard. The proconsul, Statius Quadratus, urged him to deny Christ. Think of your age, he said. Swear by the fortune of Caesar. Say, “Away with the Atheists.” Polycarp looked at the crowd, waved his hand at them and groaned. Then he looked up to heaven and said it of them: “Away with the Atheists.” Curse Christ, said the proconsul, and I will set you free. Polycarp answered that he had served Christ eighty-six years, and Christ had never done him wrong.

moments.title: Beasts, or fire
moments.text: Pressed again, he told the proconsul to stop pretending he did not know who he was: “I am a Christian. And if you wish to learn what the doctrines of Christianity are, appoint me a day, and thou shalt hear them.” The proconsul threatened him with wild beasts. Call them, said Polycarp. Then he threatened fire. “Thou threatenest me with fire which burneth for an hour, and after a little is extinguished, but art ignorant of the fire of the coming judgment and of eternal punishment, reserved for the ungodly. But why tarriest thou? Bring forth what thou wilt.” His face was “full of grace”. The herald cried three times, “Polycarp has confessed that he is a Christian.” The crowd asked for a lion. The games were over, so they shouted for fire.

miracles.lede: The letter from his church tells of wonders in the stadium. Its writers say they saw and heard them for themselves:

pledge.q: …we, to whom it was given to witness it, beheld a great miracle, and have been preserved that we might report to others what then took place.

items.title: A voice from heaven
items.text: As he entered the stadium, a voice came from heaven. No one saw who spoke. But the Christians who were there heard it.
items.quote: Be strong, Polycarp, and play the man.
items.witness: “Those of our people who were present heard the voice.”

cite.text: Martyrdom of Polycarp, chapter 9, in Lightfoot's translation (1891)

items.title: A wall of fire
items.text: The fire rose round him like a ship's sail filled with wind, and made a wall around his body. He was in the middle of it, the letter says, not like flesh burning, but like bread baking, or gold and silver glowing in a furnace.
items.quote: For the fire, shaping itself into the form of an arch, like the sail of a ship when filled with the wind, encompassed as by a circle the body of the martyr.
items.witness: The writers of the letter, who stood watching.

items.title: A sweet smell
items.text: Instead of the smell of burning, they caught a scent like incense.
items.quote: Moreover, we perceived such a sweet odour [coming from the pile], as if frankincense or some such precious spices had been smoking there.

items.title: The dove and the blood
items.text: His body would not burn. So an executioner was ordered to go close and stab him with a dagger. Out came a dove, the letter says, and so much blood that it put out the fire. The whole crowd wondered at the difference between unbelievers and the chosen.
items.quote: there came forth a dove, and a great quantity of blood, so that the fire was extinguished

note.text: Eusebius copied these chapters about 300. His copy has the voice, the fire like a sail, the sweet smell and the blood. It has no dove, and no bread.

more.title: The burning pillow
more.text: Three days before his arrest, praying at the farm, he saw his pillow on fire. He turned to those with him and said, “I must be burnt alive.” The letter says the vision came true when the crowd shouted for fire.
more.quote: the pillow under his head seemed to him on fire

more.title: A later legend: his Life
more.text: A *Life of Polycarp* under the name of Pionius was written two centuries or more after his death. It is full of wonders. As a young man, it says, he gave away his mistress's stores to the poor, and her empty storerooms filled again. When the bishops gathered to choose him, one of the brethren saw a white dove over his head. Later his prayer put out a great fire in Smyrna, and brought rain in a drought.
more.quote: One saw hovering over Polycarp's head a white dove encircled in light.

cite.text: Life of Polycarp ascribed to Pionius, chapters 4, 5, 21 and 28 to 32, tr. Lightfoot (1889)

more.title: A later legend: a voice in Rome
more.text: One manuscript, kept at Moscow, adds a note to the end of the letter. It says Irenaeus was in Rome when Polycarp died, and heard “a voice as of a trumpet” saying that Polycarp was martyred. The note says Irenaeus wrote this himself. No work of his that survives tells it, and the other manuscripts and Eusebius do not have it. Lightfoot still would not “dismiss the story at once as a pure fiction”.
more.quote: on the very day and hour when Polycarp was martyred in Smyrna

cite.text: Martyrdom of Polycarp, chapter 22, as the Moscow manuscript reads it, tr. Lightfoot (1889); Lightfoot, The Apostolic Fathers, Part 2, volume 1 (1889)

doubt.title: Doubted, and defended
doubt.text: The translators of the *Ante-Nicene Fathers* noted that Eusebius has no dove, and that “many have thought the text to be here corrupt”. One small change in the Greek gives “on the left hand side” instead of “a dove”. Bishop Lightfoot thought the dove was added by the later writer of the *Life*: “Now our spurious Pionius was before all things a miracle-monger.” Of the sweet smell, their American editor wrote that “many kinds of wood emit the like in burning”. McGiffert, who translated Eusebius, held that “Natural causes may easily have produced some such phenomena as the writers describe”. Lightfoot still defended the letter as honest. Of the voice he wrote that “the very simplicity of the narrative here disarms criticism”, since no one claimed to see the speaker. The fire like a sail, he thought, “may be explained as a strictly natural occurrence”.

cites.text: Ante-Nicene Fathers, volume 1, notes to the Martyrdom
Lightfoot, The Apostolic Fathers (1891) and Part 2, volume 1 (1889)
McGiffert, note on Eusebius, Church History, Book 4, chapter 15

words.note: One letter of his survives, the *Letter to the Philippians*. His other words were written down by his church, in the *Martyrdom*, and by Irenaeus, who heard him. Unless marked, they are in the English of Alexander Roberts and James Donaldson, as printed in the *Ante-Nicene Fathers* of 1885.

feature.q: Fourscore and six years have I been His servant, and He hath done me no wrong. How then can I blaspheme my King Who saved me?
feature.ctx: To the proconsul, who had said, “Swear the oath, and I will release thee; revile the Christ.” In J. B. Lightfoot's translation of 1891. His Greek verb, {el|δουλεύω}, is a slave's word: to serve as a slave serves.

quotes.q: To thee I have thought it right to offer an account [of my faith]; for we are taught to give all due honour (which entails no injury upon ourselves) to the powers and authorities which are ordained of God. But as for these, I do not deem them worthy of receiving any account from me.
quotes.who: To the proconsul, who told him to persuade the crowd. He would answer a governor, but not a mob.

quotes.q: …knowing that “by grace ye are saved, not of works,” but by the will of God through Jesus Christ.
quotes.who: In his *Letter*, quoting Paul to the Ephesians.

quotes.q: But He Who raised Him up from the dead will raise up us also, if we do His will, and walk in His commandments, and love what He loved.
quotes.who: On the hope of the resurrection.

quotes.q: For whosoever does not confess that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh, is antichrist.
quotes.who: Against those who said Christ only seemed to have a body. He is quoting John's first letter.

quotes.q: …not quickly crediting [an evil report] against any one, not severe in judgment, as knowing that we are all under a debt of sin. If then we entreat the Lord to forgive us, we ought also ourselves to forgive.
quotes.who: What he asked of the elders of Philippi.

quotes.q: Let us then be imitators of His patience; and if we suffer for His name's sake, let us glorify Him.
quotes.who: Written years before his own death.

extras.title: The letter from his church
extras.lede: Almost everything about his death comes from one document: a letter his church sent out after it. Eusebius knew no older account of a martyr. Roberts and Donaldson, its Victorian translators, called it “the earliest of all the Martyria”, the accounts of the martyrs.

items.title: A letter to pass on
items.text: The church of Smyrna wrote to the church at Philomelium, in Phrygia, which had asked what happened. It greets “all the congregations of the Holy and Catholic Church in every place”. A man named Evarestus wrote it. A brother carried it: Marcus in some copies, Marcianus or Marcion in others. Eusebius thought it went to Pontus, on the Black Sea. His translator guessed he misread the words “in every place” in the greeting.
items.quote: When, therefore, ye have yourselves read this Epistle, be pleased to send it to the brethren at a greater distance, that they also may glorify the Lord, Who makes such choice of His own servants.

cite.text: Martyrdom of Polycarp, greeting and chapter 20; Lightfoot (1891); Lake (1913); McGiffert, note on Eusebius, Church History, Book 4, chapter 15

items.title: A death like the Lord's
items.text: The writers say the Lord meant to show them “a martyrdom becoming the Gospel”. So they point out the likeness. His betrayers, they say, would suffer “the punishment of Judas himself”. The police captain “chanced to have the very name” of Herod. Readers have noticed more. He was taken on a Friday, by police who came “as if going out against a robber”. He rode into the city on a donkey.
items.quote: For he waited to be delivered up, even as the Lord had done, that we also might become his followers.

cite.text: Martyrdom of Polycarp, chapters 1, 6, 7 and 8; the line on Herod in Lightfoot's translation (1891)

items.title: How it reached us
items.text: Notes at the end say a man named Gaius copied it from the papers of Irenaeus. Socrates copied Gaius's copy at Corinth, and a Pionius copied that. Its translators say these notes are “no part of the original Epistle”. Eusebius copied most of the letter into his *Church History* about 300. His is the only copy older than the later editor's.
items.quote: These things Caius transcribed from the copy of Irenæus (who was a disciple of Polycarp), having himself been intimate with Irenæus.

cite.text: Martyrdom of Polycarp, chapter 22, with the translators' note; Lightfoot, The Apostolic Fathers, Part 2, volume 1 (1889)

extras.title: Where the story is argued over
extras.lede: Three questions about the *Martyrdom* are still argued over. Here they are in the words of both sides.

items.title: The Jews in the crowd
items.text: The letter names Jews four times. They are in the crowd that shouts for his death. They gather wood for the pyre, “especially, according to custom”. They press Nicetes to ask the governor not to give up the body. They watch as the Christians try to take it from the fire, and their quarrelling leads the centurion to burn it. All four lines are in Eusebius's copy too, so they are older than the later editor's notes. Older scholars took them at their word. Lightfoot, in 1889, wrote that it was a feast day, and that “the Jews were keeping holiday and busied themselves actively in the persecution”. Some scholars now doubt that this is history. The letter sets out to show a death like Christ's, and its crowd echoes the crowds of the Gospels. In the words of the Judaism and Rome project, after Lloyd Gaston, “the Jews are simply added to the crowd alongside the Gentiles”. The same commentary says the words “according to custom” give them “a direct role in his death”, as the Gospels give the crowd a role in Christ's. Bart Ehrman reads the letter as making the Jews “the enemy, more than the governor”.
items.quote: the whole multitude both of the heathen and Jews, who dwelt at Smyrna, cried out with uncontrollable fury

cite.text: Martyrdom of Polycarp, chapters 12, 13, 17 and 18; Eusebius, Church History, Book 4, chapter 15; Lightfoot (1889); Judaism and Rome, commentary; Ehrman, Forgery and Counterforgery (2013)

items.title: 155, or ten years later?
items.text: The letter names the proconsul, Statius Quadratus, and the day. Eusebius put the death under Marcus Aurelius, about 166, and Jerome followed him. In 1867 W. H. Waddington worked out when Quadratus governed Asia, from a sick man's diary. The orator Aelius Aristides had noted who governed Asia during his long illness. That gave 155. Lightfoot agreed. By 1890 McGiffert called the date “now almost universally accepted”. Two German scholars, Wieseler and Keim, still held out for 167. The churches agree on the day but not the year. Rome's calendar of 1969 says about 156. The Church of England says about 155. The Episcopal Church and the ELCA say 156. The Greek Archdiocese of America says about 163. The Coptic synaxarium says 167.
items.quote: Now the blessed Polycarp was martyred on the second day of the first part of the month Xanthicus, on the seventh before the kalends of March, on a great sabbath, at the eighth hour.

cite.text: Martyrdom of Polycarp, chapter 21, in Lightfoot's translation (1891); McGiffert, note on Eusebius, Church History, Book 4, chapter 15; Lightfoot, Part 2, volume 1 (1889); Calendarium Romanum (1969)

items.title: Was the letter added to?
items.text: All our Greek copies come through a later editor, who added his own notes at the end. Eusebius's older copy is shorter in places. In 1885 the American editor of the *Ante-Nicene Fathers* wrote, “That this Epistle has been interpolated can hardly be doubted, when we compare it with the unvarnished specimen, in Eusebius.” Some scholars go further. Candida Moss, in 2010, argued that it is not an eyewitness account. The fuller text, she said, was written long after the events, perhaps as late as the middle of the 200s. Bart Ehrman, in 2013, called it a forgery: “a legendary account written simply as if by eyewitnesses”, at least fifty years later. Others hold that it is what it says it is. McGiffert, in 1890, called its genuineness “too well established to admit of doubt”. Against the critics of his day, George Salmon wrote:
items.quote: The whole narrative of the martyrdom bears so plainly the mark of an eye-witness, that to imagine, as Lipsius and Keim have done, some one capable of inventing it a century after the death of Polycarp, seems to require great critical credulity.

cite.text: Ante-Nicene Fathers, volume 1, introductory note; Moss, Early Christianity (2010); Ehrman, Forgery and Counterforgery (2013); McGiffert, note on Eusebius, Church History, Book 4, chapter 15; Salmon, Dictionary of Christian Biography

extras.title: His prayer at the stake
extras.lede: His church gives the prayer in full. When he came to the Amen, the men lit the fire.

items.text: The whole prayer, as the letter from Smyrna gives it.
items.quote: O Lord God Almighty, the Father of Thy beloved and blessed Son Jesus Christ, by Whom we have received the knowledge of Thee, the God of angels and powers, and of every creature, and of the whole race of the righteous who live before Thee, I give Thee thanks that Thou hast counted me worthy of this day and this hour, that I should have a part in the number of Thy martyrs, in the cup of Thy Christ, to the resurrection of eternal life, both of soul and body, through the incorruption [imparted] by the Holy Ghost. Among whom may I be accepted this day before Thee as a fat and acceptable sacrifice, according as Thou, the ever-truthful God, hast foreordained, hast revealed beforehand to me, and now hast fulfilled. Wherefore also I praise Thee for all things, I bless Thee, I glorify Thee, along with the everlasting and heavenly Jesus Christ, Thy beloved Son, with Whom, to Thee, and the Holy Ghost, be glory both now and to all coming ages. Amen.

myths.truth: Probably close, but it is not what he said. He counted years of serving Christ: “Fourscore and six years have I been His servant”. Lightfoot read it as his age, “the more natural interpretation”, so born about 69 or 70. McGiffert said “we cannot tell”. But he leaned toward counting from baptism, because Polycarp spoke of serving Christ, not God.

cite.text: Martyrdom of Polycarp, chapter 9; Lightfoot (1889); McGiffert, note on Eusebius, Church History, Book 4, chapter 15

myths.claim: He was burned at the stake.
myths.truth: He was tied to a stake, and the fire was lit. The letter says the fire would not burn him. So an executioner stabbed him, and only then was his body burned. Jerome's short notice says simply “he was burned”. The Coptic synaxarium, read on his day, tells it another way: the governor “ordered to cut off his head”.

cite.text: Martyrdom of Polycarp, chapters 15, 16 and 18; Jerome, Lives of Illustrious Men, chapter 17; Coptic synaxarium, 29 Amshir

myths.truth: He was the twelfth martyr of Smyrna, “reckoning those also of Philadelphia”. The others died before him, and he died alone. The *Roman Martyrology* of 1916 has “twelve others from Philadelphia”. Most copies of Eusebius, and Rufinus's old Latin, also count twelve besides him. McGiffert thought a copyist had changed the word for twelfth into twelve.

cite.text: Martyrdom of Polycarp, chapter 19; Roman Martyrology (1916), 26 January; McGiffert, note on Eusebius, Church History, Book 4, chapter 15

myths.claim: As a boy he was a slave, bought and raised by a devout lady named Callisto.
myths.truth: This comes from the *Life of Polycarp* under the name of Pionius, written in the late 300s or later. McGiffert called it “manifestly spurious and entirely untrustworthy”. No early source says where he was born, or how he grew up.

cite.text: Life of Polycarp ascribed to Pionius, chapters 3 to 5; McGiffert, note on Eusebius, Church History, Book 4, chapter 15

myths.claim: “For 86 years I have served Jesus Christ and He has never abandoned me.”
myths.truth: A paraphrase that changes his point. He did not say Christ never left him. He said Christ never wronged him: “He hath done me no wrong”. That is why he would not curse Him.

myths.claim: “I exhort you, press on in your course, and exhort all men that they may be saved.”
myths.truth: Not his words. Ignatius wrote them to him: “I entreat thee, by the grace with which thou art clothed, to press forward in thy course, and to exhort all that they may be saved.” Quote sites list the line under Polycarp's name.

cite.text: Ignatius, Letter to Polycarp, chapter 1; AZQuotes

myths.claim: He is the “angel of the church in Smyrna” in Revelation.
myths.truth: A guess, not an early record. No early writer says so, and Revelation names no one. Archbishop Ussher suggested it in the 1600s. The editor of the *Ante-Nicene Fathers* saw “nothing improbable” in it. The Coptic synaxarium, read on his day, states it as fact.

cite.text: Ante-Nicene Fathers, volume 1, introductory note to the Letter to the Philippians; Revelation 2:8-11; Coptic synaxarium, 29 Amshir

myths.claim: He sent Benignus and other missionaries to Gaul.
myths.truth: A legend. The 1916 *Roman Martyrology* still tells it of Benignus of Dijon, of Andochius, Thyrsus and Felix of Autun, and of Andeol. The *Catholic Encyclopedia* traces the Benignus story, and others like it from Autun and nearby cities, to the early 500s. It calls them falsifications that “possess no historical value”.

cite.text: Roman Martyrology (1916); Catholic Encyclopedia (1907), “St. Benignus of Dijon”

circle.name: Irenaeus of Lyons
circle.text: Heard him as a boy in Asia, and remembered him all his life. After the *Martyrdom*, he is our main witness to Polycarp.

circle.name: Ignatius of Antioch
circle.text: The bishop of Antioch, taken through Smyrna on his way to die in Rome. He wrote Polycarp the only letter to him that survives. Polycarp gathered his letters and sent them on.

cite.text: Ignatius, Letter to Polycarp; Letter to the Philippians, chapter 13

circle.name: John
circle.text: Irenaeus calls him “John, the disciple of the Lord”. Polycarp spoke of his time with him and passed on his words. Tertullian, about 200, says the church of Smyrna “records that Polycarp was placed therein by John”. Jerome agrees. Irenaeus says only that apostles appointed him.

cite.text: Irenaeus, Against Heresies, Book 3, chapter 3; Eusebius, Church History, Book 5, chapter 20; Tertullian, Prescription against Heretics, chapter 32; Jerome, Lives of Illustrious Men, chapter 17

circle.name: Papias of Hierapolis
circle.text: Another bishop in Asia, who wrote five books. Irenaeus calls him “the hearer of John, and a companion of Polycarp”.

circle.name: Florinus
circle.text: Irenaeus, as a boy, saw him “in lower Asia with Polycarp”, a man of the royal court trying to win the old bishop's approval. He later lost his place as a presbyter at Rome, over his teaching. Irenaeus's letter to him holds his best memories of Polycarp.

cite.text: Eusebius, Church History, Book 5, chapters 15 and 20

circle.name: Anicetus
circle.text: Bishop of Rome. He and Polycarp could not agree about Easter. He still let Polycarp celebrate the Eucharist in his church.

circle.name: Marcion
circle.text: A teacher who rejected the God of the Old Testament. In Rome, Irenaeus says, Polycarp turned many of his followers back to the Church. When the two met, Polycarp called him “the first-born of Satan”.

circle.name: Germanicus
circle.text: A young Christian who faced the beasts bravely, days before Polycarp died. After his death the crowd began shouting for the old bishop.

circle.name: Herod and Nicetes
circle.text: The police captain who arrested him, and his father. They took him into their carriage and tried to talk him round. Nicetes later asked the governor to keep his body from the Christians.

circle.name: Philip of Tralles
circle.text: The Asiarch, high priest of Asia, who ran the games. The crowd asked him to set a lion on Polycarp. He refused, because the games were over. Lightfoot matched him with a Philip named on inscriptions of Tralles. His “renown had already procured for him a monument at Olympia”.

cite.text: Martyrdom of Polycarp, chapters 12 and 21; Lightfoot, The Apostolic Fathers, Part 2, volume 1 (1889)

circle.name: Alce
circle.text: A Christian woman of Smyrna whom Ignatius greeted in two letters, as “my well-beloved” and “my dearly beloved”. The *Martyrdom* calls Nicetes “brother of Alce”. Lightfoot and McGiffert think she was the same woman.

cite.text: Ignatius, Letter to the Smyrnaeans, chapter 13, and Letter to Polycarp, chapter 8; Martyrdom of Polycarp, chapter 17; McGiffert, note on Eusebius, Church History, Book 4, chapter 15

death.big: He was tied to a stake in the stadium at Smyrna on a Saturday, 23 February, most likely in 155. The fire did not burn him, so an executioner stabbed him.
paras: The crowd ran to the workshops and baths for wood. He took off his clothes and his belt. When they came to nail him to the stake, he asked them not to, and they only tied him. He put his hands behind him, bound “like a distinguished ram [taken] out of a great flock for sacrifice”. Then he looked up to heaven and prayed.

The Christians wanted his body. But Nicetes, Herod's father, asked the governor not to give it up, “lest, forsaking Him that was crucified, they begin to worship this one”. The letter answers him: “For Him indeed, as being the Son of God, we adore; but the martyrs, as disciples and followers of the Lord, we worthily love.”
The centurion had the body burned. Afterwards the Christians gathered his bones, “as being more precious than the most exquisite jewels, and more purified than gold”.

later.title: A century later
later.text: In 250, in another persecution, a Christian of Smyrna named Pionius was arrested with two companions. They were keeping the “true birth-day of the martyr Polycarp”. That year it fell on a Saturday, a high Sabbath, as it had in 155. Pionius too was put to death. Eusebius later made him a martyr of Polycarp's own day. McGiffert called that “a serious chronological blunder”. A later writer borrowed Pionius's name for the legendary *Life of Polycarp*.

cite.text: Lightfoot, The Apostolic Fathers, Part 2, volume 1 (1889), from the Acts of Pionius; McGiffert, note on Eusebius, Church History, Book 4, chapter 15

items.k: To the men with the nails
items.q: Leave me as I am; for He that giveth me strength to endure the fire, will also enable me, without your securing me by nails, to remain without moving in the pile.

saint.big: Yes. Catholics, Orthodox, Copts and Anglicans count him a saint, and Lutherans remember him too.

churches.note: A Lesser Festival in the Church of England

paras: When Rome cut back its calendar in 1969, it kept only some of the martyrs from outside Rome. The first group it kept was the famous martyrs of the early Church, {la|martyres clariores antiqui}. The group held three names: Polycarp, Perpetua and Felicity, and Cyprian.
He was honoured from the day he died. His church laid his bones in a place where it meant to meet each year, “in gladness and joy”, on the day of his death. It called that day his birthday.

The historian Arthur McGiffert called this “the earliest notice of the annual celebration of the day of a martyr's death”. The Roman calendar of 1969 quotes the same passage, to explain why saints are kept on the day they died. In the words of the letter:

quotes.q: …to celebrate the birth-day of his martyrdom for the commemoration of those that have already fought in the contest, and for the training and preparation of those that shall do so hereafter.
quotes.who: The church of Smyrna, in Lightfoot's translation (1891)

quotes.q: At Smyrna, the birthday of St. Polycarp, a disciple of the Apostle St. John, who consecrated him bishop of that city and Primate of all Asia.

prayer.title: A letter he wrote
prayer.intro: Near the end of his *Letter* he blessed the church at Philippi. Then he told them to pray, even for their persecutors.
prayer.q: But may the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, and Jesus Christ Himself, Who is the Son of God, and our everlasting High Priest, build you up in faith and truth, and in all meekness, gentleness, patience, long-suffering, forbearance, and purity; and may He bestow on you a lot and portion among His saints, and on us with you, and on all that are under heaven, who shall believe in our Lord Jesus Christ, and in His Father, Who “raised Him from the dead.” Pray for all the saints. Pray also for kings, and potentates, and princes, and for those that persecute and hate you, and for the enemies of the cross, that your fruit may be manifest to all, and that ye may be perfect in Him.
